source: Lemons, Carberry, Swan (2011) Cognitive styles and design strategies of engineering students during a hands-on model-building design task
finding: Reports the Kruger and Cross (2006) scheme: nine experienced designers, four strategies (problem driven, information driven, solution driven, knowledge driven). Only one of nine was information driven. Kruger and Cross found solution-driven designs had low overall quality and problem-driven did relatively well. Lemons applies the scheme to ten students.
numbers: Kruger and Cross sample = 9 designers (via Lemons). Lemons sample = 10 students: 6 problem driven, 3 solution driven, 1 information driven, 0 knowledge driven. Solution-driven students had very short problem analysis and poor or wrong problem representations.
quote: solution driven design seems to produce solutions of low overall quality, while problem driven design achieves relatively good results
limits: Kruger and Cross numbers are second-hand: the 2006 paper was blocked (Cloudflare) and not opened. No effect size in this source. Qualitative classification, no inferential test.
agent_relevance: The best-known 'problem-driven beats solution-driven' result rests on N=9 experts and N=10 students. Treat as a hint, not a rule, when choosing an agent order.

source: Kruger and Cross (2006) Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes, Design Studies 27(5) 527-548
finding: Abstract as returned by search: most designers used either problem-driven or solution-driven. Solution-driven designers had higher creativity scores. Problem-driven designers had the best results on most assessed solution aspects and the best balance of overall quality and creativity.
numbers: No effect sizes obtained. Sample N=9 (from d01). Full text not opened (repository returned HTTP 403, core.ac.uk returned a Cloudflare challenge page).
quote: Designers using a solution driven strategy had higher creativity scores
limits: Gap 3 stays open on effect size. New nuance: solution-driven designers scored higher on CREATIVITY, so the trade-off is quality versus creativity, not a plain loss.
agent_relevance: A solution-first order may buy novelty and cost fit. Test both outcomes (correctness and diversity), not one score.

source: Studer, Daly, McKilligan, Seifert (2018) Evidence of problem exploration in creative designs, AIEDAM 32:415-430
finding: Large qualitative study of 252 problems from award-winning products and open design competitions. Designers reframed the presented problem in 32 distinct patterns. More exploration patterns in the discovered problem went with placing higher in the challenge. Designers often narrowed the problem (specific function, setting or stakeholder).
numbers: 252 design problems; 32 exploration patterns; two independent coders; r(102) = -0.18, p < 0.05 between number of patterns and placement; all 19 finalists had 2 or more patterns; the 5 solutions with a single pattern were not finalists or semifinalists.
limits: Small correlation on a subset (df 102). Non-experimental, competition entries, no expert-novice split. Authors say the link to outcome still needs study.
agent_relevance: Closest large-N data for gap 8 and gap 10: reframing the problem, not only solving it, goes with better-placed designs, with a small effect. Supports a reframing operator.

source: Studer et al. (2018) discussion: problem exploration as narrowing
finding: Authors state that designers often choose to narrow the problem space rather than broaden it, which cuts against a simple breadth-first story for experts.
numbers: Same data set as d03 (252 problems). No group-level breadth percentages recovered in the sections read.
limits: Competition entries only; novices not identified separately.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'widen the problem first'. Allow a narrowing step after exploration.

source: Ball and Christensen (2019) Advancing an understanding of design cognition and design metacognition, Design Studies
finding: Review says expert designers jump toward solution ideas rather than formulating the whole problem up front, and treat even well-defined problems as ill-defined, relaxing or redefining constraints.
numbers: No new numbers; cites Eastman 1970, Lawson 1979, Lloyd and Scott 1994.
quote: experienced designers still treat well-defined design problems as if they are ill-defined
limits: Review. The claim about well-defined problems is asserted; no direct manipulation of definedness in this text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: still no experiment that varies definedness. 'Experts reframe even well-defined problems' suggests an agent should be allowed to question constraints in every task type.

source: Cross (2001/2004) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies (Georgia Tech copy)
finding: Gives the Lawson 1979 summary used in the field. Scientists tried to find the problem structure; architects generated high-scoring solutions until one was acceptable. Lawson repeated the experiment with first-year science and architecture students and found no such difference. Lloyd and Scott (1994): more experienced designers used more generative reasoning; specific experience of the problem type enabled conjectural design.
numbers: No group sizes, scores or tests given for Lawson. Lawson 1979 is cited as Ergonomics 22(1):59-68; the paper was paywalled and not opened.
quote: It appears to be a difference that grows with education and experience in designing.
limits: Gap 2 stays open: group sizes and significance of Lawson (1979) and any later professional follow-up were not found in any open source. Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: The Lawson effect depends on experience, so it is a learned habit; the agent test should be 'does a solution-first scaffold help', not 'is the model naturally solution-focused'.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Closest direct LLM analogue of the Lawson hidden-rule task (a Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery loop). Eleven LLMs propose test triples, get feedback, guess the rule. LLMs show confirmation bias (too many tests that fit the current guess). Less bias went with higher success, and thinking-mode models did better on both.
numbers: Task success 6% to 78% across model-inference scenarios within 45 interactions. Counterexample interventions (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites) raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. 80 test episodes per cell; paired permutation tests (50,000), Benjamini-Hochberg. Gains significant for thinking models, mixed for non-thinking models.
limits: Number triples, not design. It tests hypothesis-testing strategy (falsify vs confirm), not 'write a solution first'. Models: Qwen3 8B/14B/32B, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly answered by analogy. A guess-first loop is what these agents do anyway; the failure is that they only confirm. A solution-first order needs a rule to deliberately test against the candidate, not just write it. The direct solution-first vs constraints-first comparison at equal tokens was not found.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) distillation and transfer results
finding: Fine-tuning Qwen3 models on intervention-guided traces cut confirmation bias and generalised to the Blicket test and to retries on math (AIME 2025, Beyond AIME). Cross-scale intervention distillation almost tripled task success for the 8B student.
numbers: Training 1,600 episodes from 4 rule sets; validation 16; test 80. Distilled models showed at most 2% degradation on other abilities in the sanity check.
limits: Fine-tuning, not scaffolding alone; small open models.
agent_relevance: A falsification habit transfers across hypothesis tasks. A scaffold operator 'seek a test that would break my current candidate' has LLM support.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: evaluating inductive reasoning in LLMs with rule discovery games
finding: Twelve LLMs on a Wason 2-4-6 style game with semantic rules. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones. The main driver of success was negative testing (trying to falsify). Failures were tied to patterns in how models navigate the hypothesis space.
numbers: Best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41% success; GPT-5.2-Chat 75%; GPT-OSS-120B 68%; other instruction-tuned models 33-35%; GPT-5-Nano 12%; Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation-bias ratios 39.0% (GPT-5-Mini), 27.3% (GPT-5.2-Chat) versus 66-82% for instruction-tuned models. Oracle agreement 85-95%.
limits: Word-category rules, not design. Same model served as player and oracle in some analyses.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered only for hypothesis testing: current reasoning models (GPT-5.2) are far from optimal. No 2025-26 frontier study of design fixation itself was found.

source: Hu, Long, Wang (2026) When continual learning moves to memory: a study of experience reuse in LLM agents
finding: Compares raw trajectory memory (concrete cases) with Insight memory (LLM-abstracted strategies) in ALFWorld and BabyAI. Abstract insights transferred across tasks more reliably; raw trajectories helped within-task but gave negative transfer across tasks, mostly on hard cases.
numbers: A to B direction, forward transfer: ALFWorld Raw -9.5 vs Insight +6.5; BabyAI Raw -7.5 vs Insight +9.0. Task A success ALFWorld Raw 80.5 vs Insight 65.5. ALFWorld Raw: retention +4.6 but new-learning -26.1 on hard cases. Qwen-Plus backbone, two runs per condition.
limits: One backbone, two environments, few runs. Not design tasks. Raw cases win when the new task matches the old.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly answered: abstract schemas are safer across tasks; concrete cases are better when the new problem is close. Same direction as the schema-vs-case split in Ball et al. A hybrid with similarity-gated retrieval is the safe design.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart: early failure prediction and restart for SWE agentic tasks
finding: A 0.6B monitor predicts failure of a coding-agent run and triggers a fresh same-policy rollout, optionally with the old diff offered as overlay. Restart with carry-over beat cold restart.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified. At 25% false-positive target, Qwen3.6-27B resolution 66.6% to 71.8% with RestartSmart versus 66.8% for cold restart. At 5% FPR saves 14.6-20.4% of tokens (20.4% on Qwen3.6-27B vs 12.5% for a per-step baseline).
limits: A learned monitor, not a simple 'persist k tries' rule; not tested on the Ege et al. hackathon failure; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 in part: restart helps only when something useful crosses the boundary. A pivot rule should carry forward what was learned, not start empty.

source: TraceML (2026) What auto-research agents miss in long-horizon ML development
finding: Compares 4,465 human Kaggle trajectories (134 competitions) with two agent scaffolds on 7 competitions (430 human vs 207 agent trajectories). Agents pivot at the wrong rate and almost never return to an abandoned approach. A short planning prompt distilled from human practice moves behaviour toward the human profile and lifts scores.
numbers: Pivot rate: humans 25%, Codex 9%, MLEvolve 58%. Matched on code state, Codex is out-pivoted about 3 to 1. Mean score effect of the three steps after a pivot: matched humans +0.089, MLEvolve -0.008. Top humans return to earlier work on 9% of eligible versions; 78% of returns end above the version returned to; Codex returned once, MLEvolve never.
limits: Kaggle ML tasks, two scaffolds, 7 shared competitions. Planning-prompt effect size not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: best outside-the-hackathon evidence that agents pivot badly (too little, or too much without gain) and cannot reopen abandoned lines. Supports a pivot-with-return operator: park an idea with a note, allow reopening.

source: Jackson, Liebel, Prikladnicki, van der Hoek (2026) Exploring creativity in human-human-LLM collaborative software design
finding: 18 pairs of software professionals designed a system in 90 minutes with optional LLM access. Creativity appeared in all pairs; 13 of 18 design documents had it. Mostly credited to humans. The LLM rarely reshaped the problem space and mostly helped on solutions; sometimes it added complexity or digressions.
numbers: 18 pairs (36 participants); 90 minutes; 13 of 18 design documents contained creativity; no instance found of the LLM reshaping the problem space.
limits: LLM was ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo (old). Qualitative. Not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 7: LLMs did not reframe the problem unprompted, so co-evolution has to be scaffolded. No test of forced alternation was found.

source: Lyu, Kim, Xiao, Luan (2026) Why LLMs and humans converge and diverge in evaluating creativity
finding: Six LLMs rated creative ideas. Agreement with humans was moderate, strongest on novelty and weakest on contextual (market, social) aspects. LLM ratings did not move when contextual information was added; human ratings did.
numbers: Study 2: 1,103 ideas from 293 people; Pearson r = 0.50 between aggregate LLM and human ratings. Study 3: N = 1,195 participants; context effect on humans b = 0.18, SE 0.04, p < 0.001; no LLM showed a significant effect. Models: GPT-4.1 mini, Grok 4 Fast, DeepSeek V3, ERNIE 3.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini.
limits: Everyday and product ideas, not expert designer ratings; no calibration procedure tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: an uncalibrated LLM judge tracks novelty but is blind to context, which is the design part. Not safe as a stop rule alone.

source: Creativity Benchmark (2025) a benchmark for marketing creativity for LLMs
finding: Three LLM-as-judge setups compared with human rankings gave weak, inconsistent correlations and judge-specific biases. Prior studies it cites report limited agreement.
numbers: Prior-work figures quoted in the paper: Kendall tau about 0.50; task-wise Pearson from about -0.21 to 1.00 depending on task and prompt set.
limits: Marketing tasks. A calibrated judge was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no study found that calibrates an LLM judge to expert DESIGN ratings and then tests it as a stopping rule. Keep a rubric or human check.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding design fixation in generative AI (re-opened for gap 4)
finding: Defines GenAI design fixation and runs an experiment on text and image models. Already used in K10. Re-opened to check whether reasoning models were tested: the abstract and framing report no o1-class or GPT-5-class models.
numbers: Numbers as in the c-series (67.4% vs 78.2% unique terms etc.).
limits: 2024-generation models; confirms gap 4 remains open for reasoning models. Only the abstract and opening pages were checked for model names.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 remains open: no published fixation measure for current reasoning models was found.

source: Atman et al. (2007) Engineering design processes: students and expert practitioners (J Eng Educ 96(4):359-379)
finding: Search showed only bibliographic detail and a companion note that freshmen reached later stages less often and spent less time evaluating. The 19/26/24 sample counts could not be verified; a 2005 expert paper in the same group had 18 experts.
numbers: Unverified: 19 experts, 26 freshmen, 24 seniors. Mosborg et al. 2005: 18 experts.
limits: Not opened; remains snippet-level. Do not use the 19/26/24 figure as fact.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no human expert-novice sample of 30 or more per group was found. The largest known (Atman) is about 20-26 per group if the counts are right.
